metaDescription: Understand adopted child and stepchild property rights in India. Learn why adopted children inherit equally while stepchildren need a Will to inherit.
author: Advocate Sneha Jaiswal
governingLawPlainEnglish: Explain the sharp contrast in simple everyday language: (1) Adopted Child: under Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (and Juvenile Justice Act adoption orders), a legally adopted child has 100% the exact same Class I inheritance and ancestral coparcenary rights as a biological child. (2) Stepchild (your spouse's child from an earlier marriage whom you have not formally adopted): under Section 8 and Section 15 of the Hindu Succession Act (as confirmed by the Supreme Court in Lachman Singh), a stepchild is NOT a legal heir to a step-parent's property! If a stepfather or stepmother wants their stepchild to receive anything, they MUST write a Will.

title: How to Include Pet Care, Charity & Caretakers in an Indian Will
subtitle: Why you cannot name a dog or cat as a bank beneficiary in India, and the exact Caretaker Fund clause that protects your pets and charities.
metaDescription: Learn how to include pet care and charity in a Will in India. See sample clauses for pet caretakers, NGO or temple donations, and loyal household staff.
author: Advocate Sneha Jaiswal
governingLawPlainEnglish: Explain in simple, friendly everyday words: under Indian law, a pet (dog, cat, bird) cannot open a bank account or be named as a direct legal beneficiary. If you write 'I leave Rs 5 Lakhs to my dog Bruno', that gift fails! Instead, you name a trusted human 'Pet Caretaker' in your Will and leave a specific sum (or conditional bequest) to that person for feeding, vet care, and housing your pet. For charities, temples, or NGOs, explain that you now have 100% freedom across all communities (after the Supreme Court struck down old Section 118 restrictions in John Vallamattom), provided you write the NGO/Trust's exact registered name, registration number, and PAN.

metaTitle: Is a Handwritten Will Valid in India? Holographic Guide
title: Is a Handwritten (Holographic) Will Valid in India? Rules & Risks
subtitle: Yes, a Will written by hand in a notebook is valid in India - but unlike some Western countries, it STILL fails without two witnesses.
metaDescription: Is a handwritten Will valid in India? Yes, courts trust handwritten Wills, but Section 63 still requires 2 witnesses. Compare handwritten vs typed Wills.
author: Advocate Sunita Deshmukh
governingLawPlainEnglish: Explain clearly in simple language: Yes, a Will written completely in your own handwriting (called a 'holographic Will') is 100% legally valid in India under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and Indian courts actually respect it because it is very hard for anyone to fake an entire page of your handwriting. HOWEVER, warn readers about two fatal mistakes: (1) Unlike some US states or European countries where a handwritten Will needs no witnesses, in India a handwritten Will WITHOUT 2 adult witnesses signing it is 100% INVALID! (2) Handwritten Wills written without a checklist often forget the Residuary Clause, exact property numbers, or accidentally use unclear language. Show why a guided online typed Will (plus a 2-line handwritten note at the bottom in your own hand!) gives you the best of both worlds.
